intro: A multiple integral adds up a quantity spread over an area or a volume, such as the total rain falling on a field or the mass of an object. This branch extends integration (adding up many tiny pieces) to two and three dimensions.

VII.13.01.what: A double integral adds up values over a rectangle, and can be pictured as the volume under a surface, like soil piled on a garden bed.

levels.a: Interprets a double integral as the volume under a surface.
levels.b: Estimates it by adding up many thin boxes.
levels.d: Estimates a double integral from a table of values.

VII.13.02.what: Iterated integrals compute a double integral as two ordinary integrals, one inside the other.

levels.a: Does the inner integral first, then the outer one.
levels.b: Uses the fact that the order can be swapped over a rectangle.
levels.d: Splits products of separate x and y parts into two simple integrals.

VII.13.03.what: Integrating over regions with curved edges, not just rectangles.

levels.a: Handles regions between two curves stacked top and bottom.
levels.b: Handles regions between two curves side by side.
levels.c: Finds the correct limits from a sketch of the region.
levels.d: Evaluates the integral over such regions.

VII.13.04.what: Swapping the order of integration can turn an impossible integral into an easy one.

levels.a: Sketches the region from the given limits.
levels.b: Rewrites the limits for the other order.
levels.c: Explains why switching order can help.
levels.d: Solves integrals that look impossible in their original order.

VII.13.05.what: Using distance and angle (polar coordinates) instead of x and y, which suits circles and round regions.

levels.a: Learns how a small area piece looks in polar coordinates.
levels.b: Converts both the region and the function to polar form.
levels.d: Evaluates the famous bell-curve integral using polar coordinates.

VII.13.06.what: Using double integrals to find real quantities such as area, mass, balance points and probabilities.

levels.a: Finds areas and masses of flat plates.
levels.b: Finds the balance point (center of mass).
levels.c: Finds how hard an object is to spin (moment of inertia).
levels.d: Finds probabilities involving two random quantities.

VII.13.07.what: Triple integrals add up a quantity throughout a solid, such as the total mass of an object with uneven density.

levels.a: Uses triple integrals to find volume and mass.
levels.b: Sets up limits for a solid region.
levels.c: Knows the six possible orders of integrating and when to switch.

VII.13.08.what: Using coordinate systems that suit round shapes: cylindrical for cans and pipes, spherical for balls and cones.

levels.a: Uses cylindrical coordinates: a polar angle and distance plus height.
levels.b: Uses spherical coordinates: distance from center plus two angles.
levels.c: Uses the correct small-volume piece in each system.
levels.d: Chooses the best coordinate system for a given problem.

VII.13.09.what: Changing variables reshapes an awkward region into a simple one, with a correction factor (the Jacobian) for how areas stretch.

levels.a: Learns what the Jacobian measures: how much the change stretches area.
levels.b: Computes the Jacobian as a determinant.
levels.c: Transforms a region into a simpler shape.
levels.d: Evaluates an integral after changing variables.
